windsor.intro: An oak said to be 900 years old stands near Snow Hill in Windsor Great Park, and it has a bronze double in the Savill Garden visitor centre. The Signing Oak was 9.55 metres round when the Tree Register recorded it in 2008. Its name comes from 1972, when, by the account attached to it, a Statement of Intent recognising the park as a conservation area was signed beneath it. Reaching it takes about an hour on foot down the Long Walk from Windsor.
windsor.meta_description: The Signing Oak in Windsor Great Park is said to be 900 years old and 9.55 metres round. A bronze replica of it stands at the Savill Garden.
windsor.question_meta: Windsor's oldest mapped tree is the Signing Oak in Windsor Great Park, said to be 900 years old and 9.55 metres round in 2008.
windsor.question_answer: Windsor's oldest mapped tree is the Signing Oak, a Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur) near Snow Hill in Windsor Great Park. Windsor Great Park and the Queen's Green Canopy put it at 900 years; a print listing says 800, and neither figure comes with a method.
windsor.question_context: The oak was 9.55 metres round when the Tree Register recorded it in 2008, a trunk about three metres across. It stands in open parkland at the south-west corner of the wood north of Snow Hill, roughly 500 metres west-north-west of the Copper Horse statue. The Queen's Green Canopy named it one of its 70 Ancient Trees in 2022, and a bronze replica made from scans of the living tree stands in The Gallery Cafe at the Savill Garden visitor centre. The name comes from 1972, when, by the account attached to it, a Statement of Intent recognising the park as a conservation area was signed beneath it. Neither age comes with a method, so read either as an estimate, which would put its first leaves in the twelfth or early thirteenth century. The park is free and open daily from dawn to dusk, and the Tree Register records this oak as open access on Crown Estate land. From Windsor it is about an hour on foot down the Long Walk.

faq.q: How old is the Signing Oak?
faq.a: Windsor Great Park and the Queen's Green Canopy say 900 years; a print listing says 800. Neither figure comes with a method, so it is an estimate.

faq.q: Why is it called the Signing Oak?
faq.a: By the account attached to it, a Statement of Intent recognising the park as a conservation area was signed beneath it in 1972.

faq.q: How do you get to it from Windsor?
faq.a: Walk the Long Walk to Snow Hill, about an hour from the Windsor stations. The oak is roughly 500 metres west-north-west of the Copper Horse statue.
